newsitem.title: USA: Fla. plaintiffs build case on smoke, disease.
newsitem.headline: Fla. plaintiffs build case on smoke, disease.

text.p: Plaintiffs in a landmark flight attendants' lawsuit against the tobacco industry built their case Wednesday that secondhand smoke causes disease, questioning a cardiologist who said years of research had shown a link between smoke and sickness in non-smokers.

"I don't think there is any significant controversy about whether the effect is there, that is that secondhand smoke causes heart disease, no," said Dr. John Holbrook, a cardiologist and Chief of the Division of General and Internal Medicine at the University of Utah School of Medicine.

The case, known as Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, is in its third week of testimony and is expected to continue through the summer. The $5 billion class action was brought on behalf of thousands of flight attendants who say they were sickened by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke while working on U.S. passenger jets.
The trial in Dade County Circuit Court is both the first class action and the first secondhand smoke action against big tobacco to come before a jury.
By Wednesday the plaintiffs' attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, had called about a third of some 40 witnesses on their list, although they have said they will not call all of them.

During cross-examination, David Hardy, an attorney for Philip Morris and Lorillard Inc., questioned Holbrook closely about when he felt comfortable saying secondhand smoke causes heart disease. He cited Holbrook's comment that he had been convinced by a major study of the effect of secondhand smoke on nurses released this spring.
"Until May 1997, as far as you, Dr. Holbrook, were concerned, there was a real scientific controversy as to whether environmental tobacco smoke causes coronary heart disease," Hardy asked.
Holbrook replied that he disagreed with Hardy's wording.

"Up until earlier this year, I considered environmental tobacco smoke to be a major risk factor. And that's a semantic that may not be easily appreciated by those outside the field, but it's a development of increasing evidence. ... It's not as if I suddenly changed my mind," he said.
After the plaintiffs rest, attorneys for the nine defendants -- seven tobacco companies and two industry trade groups -- will begin calling their slate of witnesses, which also number about 40.
The tobacco defendants say the incidence of lung cancer and other ailments among the flight attendants was no greater than that of other groups of nonsmokers.
